samples.text:
These days, many people use technology like Google or GPS apps instead of remember information by themselves. This essay will discuss why this happen and how it affects people's ability to think independently.

There are some reasons for this situation. The main reason is that technology is very convenient and fast. If someone want to know the capital of a country or a recipe, they can find the answer in a few seconds on their smartphone. In the past, people had to go to library or ask other people, which took long time. Another reason is that modern life is very busy and there is too much information to remember, so people prefer to let their phone remember it for them. For example, most people today do not remember phone numbers of their friends because they are saved in the phone.

In my opinion, this trend has a negative effect on people's ability to think by themselves. When people always use navigation apps, they do not learn the roads in their city, and if the phone battery is finish they can get lost easily. Similarly, students who copy answers from the internet do not really understand the topic and they cannot solve problems without help. However, technology can also have some positive effect, because people can find more information and compare different ideas quickly.

In conclusion, people depend on technology because it is quick and easy and life is busy. Although it has some benefits, I believe that it mostly makes people less able to think independently, so people should try to use their own brain more often.
samples.why: Both questions addressed with a clear view · examples relevant but general · repetitive linking and word choice (people, think) · several errors with verb forms and articles that do not impede communication.

samples.text:
In recent years, people have become increasingly dependent on digital tools such as search engines and GPS applications to answer questions and find their way. This essay will explain why this shift has occurred and argue that, while it frees people from memorising facts, it can weaken their capacity for independent thought.

The main reason for this dependence is the sheer convenience of modern technology. With a smartphone in almost every pocket, any piece of information can be retrieved within seconds, so there seems little point in storing it in one's own memory. Why would a driver study a map when an app can calculate the fastest route and warn about traffic in real time? In addition, the amount of information people are expected to deal with has grown enormously, and handing routine facts over to devices allows them to cope with a demanding lifestyle. Many people no longer even know their close family members' phone numbers.

The effect on independent thinking is, in my view, largely negative. When answers are always available instantly, people have fewer reasons to work through a problem, evaluate evidence or remember what they have learnt. A student who immediately searches online for the solution to a maths question may get the correct answer but gains little understanding of the method behind it. Moreover, search engines rank results according to algorithms, so users often accept the first information they see without questioning its reliability. That said, technology can support critical thinking if it is used as a starting point for research rather than a substitute for it.

To conclude, people rely on technology because it is fast, convenient and helps them manage information overload. However, this habit can reduce people's ability to analyse and remember, and individuals should make conscious effort to think problems through before reaching for their phones.
samples.why: Clear position throughout · both questions answered with extended examples · logical paragraphing and varied cohesive devices · good collocation (information overload, sheer convenience) · occasional slip such as a missing article.

samples.text:
Few people today would set off for an unfamiliar destination without a navigation app, and even fewer would try to recall an obscure fact when a search engine can supply it instantly. This growing reliance on technology stems largely from its convenience and ubiquity, and although it has clear benefits, I believe it risks eroding people's capacity to think independently.

The shift can be explained by several interrelated factors. The most obvious is accessibility: smartphones have placed vast quantities of information within constant reach, making the effort of memorisation seem unnecessary. At the same time, the pace of modern life encourages people to delegate routine mental tasks. A commuter juggling work messages and family arrangements has little incentive to learn a route by heart when an app will not only guide them but also adjust for traffic. Furthermore, these tools are generally accurate, so people have come to trust them more than their own, sometimes unreliable, recollection.

The consequences for independent thought are more troubling. Memory and reasoning are closely linked; people who store knowledge internally are better able to make connections, spot inconsistencies and form original judgements. When everything is looked up on demand, this internal framework is never built. Navigation offers a telling example: drivers who follow turn-by-turn instructions often develop little sense of how a city fits together and can become disoriented as soon as the signal drops. More broadly, search engines present information that has already been filtered and ranked, which can encourage passive acceptance rather than critical evaluation. Admittedly, technology can also stimulate thinking by exposing users to a wider range of sources, but this depends on people actively questioning what they find.

In conclusion, dependence on digital tools has arisen because they are fast, reliable and constantly available. While they undoubtedly save time, habitual reliance on them can weaken memory and discourage critical reasoning, so they are best treated as aids to thinking rather than replacements for it.
samples.why: Both questions fully developed with a nuanced, consistent position · ideas logically sequenced and well supported · sophisticated vocabulary used precisely (ubiquity, delegate, disoriented) · varied, virtually error-free complex structures.
